opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm pretty enthusiastic about it. Part of why we publish the data is so that other people can look at it in ways we didn't think of, or ask questions we didn't have time to ask. We're a small team, and there are far more interesting cuts of the data than we could ever write up ourselves. So if someone wants to dig in and say, "What do the people who think X believe about Y?", that seems great to me.

Filtering respondents based on their answers is a reasonable thing to want to do. For instance, you might ask whether the people who seem to have thought hardest about AI timelines, or who give internally consistent answers, look different from everyone else. That's a legitimate question. I'd just encourage people to be careful and transparent about it. Once you start choosing which respondents count based on what they said, it becomes easy, even without meaning to, to end up with a subset that tells the story you already believed. Say clearly what you filtered on and why, ideally decide that before looking at the results, and show how sensitive the conclusions are to the choice.

It's also worth keeping in mind that some of the apparent "inconsistency" in the responses is itself informative. When people give quite different answers depending on how a question is framed, that tells you something real about how uncertain and unsettled people's views are. That might not be noise you want to filter out. It might be one of the main findings.

So overall: please do reanalyze it, I'm glad when people do. Just be thoughtful about the choices, and present the results so readers can tell what's coming from the respondents and what's coming from the analyst's decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says the team could write up only a fraction of the many interesting ways to analyze the data, communicating that the published analysis covers only a small part of what could be learned.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm pretty happy about it. We put the data out there precisely so people could look at it themselves, and I'd much rather have people poking at it and arguing about what it means than just citing a headline number. The whole point of releasing it is that we don't have a monopoly on the right way to interpret it.

That said, I think there's a distinction worth drawing. Reanalysis in general is great. Filtering respondents based on their answers is where I get a bit more cautious. If you say, "let's only look at the people who think X," you're partly just reading off your selection criterion again. You can end up with something that looks like a finding but is mostly an artifact of who you kept. So I'd want people to be clear about what question they're actually answering when they do that. "What do researchers who already think AI is risky believe about timelines?" is a fine question. It's just a different question from "what do AI researchers believe?"

The other thing I'd say is that the survey has a lot of noise and framing effects in it, which we've been fairly upfront about. People give wildly different answers depending on how you phrase the question about, say, high-level machine intelligence versus full automation of labor. So anyone slicing it finely should expect that the slices are even noisier than the whole. I'd be wary of anyone drawing sharp conclusions from small subgroups.

But overall, yes, please do it. I'd rather be in a world where the data gets scrutinized, including in ways I might disagree with, than one where everyone just takes our summary at face value. If someone finds we made a mistake, I'd genuinely want to know.

r001.rationale: The response welcomes reanalysis and says the data can be interpreted in different ways, but it does not state that the published analysis covers only a small part of what could be learned from the data.

astra-6.text: I’m generally very happy for people to reanalyze the data. There are lots of questions you could ask that we haven’t explored, and I don’t think our analysis should be the last word. Filtering respondents can be useful, but it matters what you’re trying to learn and why you chose that filter. If you exclude people because their answers seem implausible to you, you risk building your own views into the result. You’re then answering a question about a selected subset of researchers, rather than researchers overall. I’d want that distinction to be clear, and ideally to see how much the conclusions depend on the filtering choices.

r001.rationale: The response says there are many questions the researchers have not explored and that their analysis should not be the last word, conveying that the published analysis covers only part of what the data could reveal.

sol-6.1.text: I’m generally happy for people to reanalyze the data. Part of the point of making it public is that people can ask different questions or notice things we missed. Filtering respondents can make sense, but it depends on what you’re trying to learn and why you think those answers are grounds for exclusion. If you filter people out because you disagree with their views, you may end up answering a different question from what AI researchers broadly think. So I’d want the filtering criteria to be explicit, and ideally to see how much the results change with and without them.

r001.rationale: The response welcomes people asking different questions and noticing things the authors missed, but it does not state that the published analysis covers only a small part of what the data could reveal.
